title: Quote the Literal: Numbers Stored as Strings
description: Querying a VARCHAR column with a numeric literal converts the column and abandons the index; quote the value so it stays a string seek. Why it matters: numeric-looking identifiers stored as text (account numbers, codes) are common in real schemas, and this exact mismatch is a frequent, invisible performance trap.
narrative:
## What This Lesson Is About
This lesson is a close cousin of the earlier implicit-conversion lesson, focused specifically on the common real-world habit of storing numeric-looking values — like account numbers — as text. It shows how comparing that text column to a plain numeric literal can quietly disable a perfectly good index.

Why does this happen? SQL Server has a strict pecking order of data types, and numbers always outrank text in that order. So when you write `WHERE AccountNumber = 4001234` and `AccountNumber` is actually a `VARCHAR` column, SQL Server doesn't convert your number to text (which would be free and harmless) — it insists on converting the *column's* text values to numbers instead, one row at a time, before it can compare anything. That row-by-row conversion means the sorted index on the text values becomes useless.

Picture an index sorted alphabetically as text: "4001234" sorts differently than the number 4001234 would in numeric order (imagine "40" coming right after "39" alphabetically instead of after "4000000"). Because SQL Server has decided to treat everything as numbers for the comparison, it can't trust that alphabetical sort order anymore — it has to recheck every single row after converting it. The simple fix: write your literal as text too — `WHERE AccountNumber = '4001234'` — so the comparison matches the column's real type and the index stays usable.

## Scenario
Account numbers are stored as text (`AccountNumber VARCHAR(20)`) with a unique index. A lookup for one account scans all 200,000 rows to return a single row — even though the index exists.

## Why it's slow
The query compares the column to a **numeric literal**: `WHERE AccountNumber = 4001234`. `INT` has **higher datatype precedence** than `VARCHAR`, so SQL Server converts the *column* to `INT` on every row: `CONVERT_IMPLICIT(INT, AccountNumber)`. A converted column can't be seeked, so the index is abandoned for an **Index Scan**.

## What to look for
- An Index Scan (not a Seek) on a unique index, returning one row after reading everything.
- A `CONVERT_IMPLICIT` on `AccountNumber` in the predicate.

## The concept
Match the literal's type to the column's. Quote it — `WHERE AccountNumber = '4001234'` — so the comparison stays `VARCHAR`-to-`VARCHAR` and the engine seeks straight to the row. The broader lesson: if a column stores digits as text, always search it with a **string** literal (and parameterize as a string in your app).
hints: The index exists but the plan scans. A numeric literal vs a VARCHAR column forces a conversion.
INT outranks VARCHAR, so the COLUMN gets converted to INT on every row, disqualifying the seek.
Quote the value so it's a string literal matching the column: WHERE AccountNumber = '4001234'.
